p: בְּהַפְטָרַת שַׁבָּת חֲנוּכָּה וְהִנֵּה מְנוֹרַת זָהָב כֻּלָּהּ וְגוּלָּה עַל רֹאשָׁהּ וְשִׁבְעָה נֵרוֹתֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ וְגוֹמֵר,
— In the haftarah of Shabbat Chanukah: “Behold, a menorah entirely of gold, with its bowl upon its top and its seven lamps upon it,” and so forth.
וּבַפְּסִיקְתָּא (פָּרָשָׁה ח׳) וְהִנֵּה מְנוֹרַת זָהָב כֻּלָּהּ זוֹ כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
— The Pesikta, section 8, explains: “‘Behold, a menorah entirely of gold’—this is the Community of Israel,” and so forth;
וְגוּלָּה עַל רֹאשָׁהּ זֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵי,
— “‘with its bowl upon its top’—this is the Holy One, blessed be He,” and so forth;
וְשִׁבְעָה נֵרוֹתֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ זְכוּת הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל מְשַׁמְּרִים אֶחָד לְשִׁבְעָה יָמִים.
— “‘and its seven lamps upon it’—the merit of Shabbat, which Israel observes one day in seven.”

p: הַיְינוּ כִּי מְנוֹרָה הִיא הַכְּלִי הַמְקַבֶּלֶת הַשֶּׁמֶן בְּתוֹכָהּ וּמְרַמֶּזֶת עַל כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הַמְקַבֶּלֶת הַשְׁפָּעַת הַדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה מֵהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
— The menorah is the vessel that receives the oil, alluding to the Community of Israel, which receives the flow of Torah teachings from the Holy One, blessed be He.

וְזָהָב מְרַמֵּז שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה עִם יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם כִּי זָהָב מְרַמֵּז מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה כַּיָּדוּעַ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר מִצָּפוֹן זָהָב יֶאֱתֶה וְשֻׁלְחָן בַּצָּפוֹן שֶׁמִּצַּד הַיִּרְאָה מַמְשִׁיךְ עֲשִׁירוּת,
— Gold alludes to studying Torah with fear of Heaven, since gold signifies awe, as is known. Thus it says, “From the north comes gold,” and the Table stood in the north: awe draws down wealth.
וְהַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִדַּת מַלְכוּת מִדַּת יִרְאָה וְנֶאֱמַר יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ שֶׁהִיא הָאוֹצָר לְהַחֲזִיק הַדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה,
— The Community of Israel corresponds to Malkhut, the attribute of awe. “Fear of Hashem is His treasury”: it is the storehouse that retains Torah teachings.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ל׳) יֵשׁ לְךָ אַפּוֹתִיקָאוֹת לְהַכְנִיס הַתְּבוּאָה וְהַשֶּׁמֶן עַיֵּן שָׁם,
— As stated in Shemot Rabbah, chapter 30, “Do you have storehouses in which to put the grain and oil?” See there.
וְכֵן הַשֶּׁמֶן שֶׁהִיא חָכְמָה כְּדְאִיתָא (מְנָחוֹת פה:) הוּא תּוֹךְ הַמְּנוֹרַת זָהָב שֶׁהִיא הָאִשָּׁה יִרְאַת הַשֵּׁם דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרְאָה כֵּן.
— Likewise, the oil, which signifies wisdom, as taught in Menachot 85b, is held within the golden menorah, “the woman who fears Hashem,” a designation of the Community of Israel.
וְגוּלָּה עַל רֹאשָׁהּ מְרַמֵּז עַל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁמַּשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם הַדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה.
— “With its bowl upon its top” alludes to the Holy One, blessed be He, who bestows Torah teachings upon them.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עַל רֹאשָׁהּ דְּהַיְינוּ הִתְחַדְּשׁוּת דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁמִּצַּד טַלָּא דְּעַתִּיק שֶׁהוּא עַל הָרֹאשׁ לְמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגַת שֵׂכֶל אֱנוֹשִׁיִּי,
— “Upon its top” signifies new Torah insights that come from the dew of Atik, above the head, beyond human intellectual comprehension.

וְכַדִּכְתִיב וְשִׁבְעָה מוּצָקוֹת לַנֵּרוֹת שֶׁשּׁוֹפְעוֹת וְנוֹזֵל הַשֶּׁמֶן מֵעַצְמָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים שֶׁכֵּן עִנְיַן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ הַחֲכָמִים מְחַדְּשִׁים הַדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה וּבֶאֱמֶת הֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים.

— As it is written, “and seven conduits for the lamps,” from which the oil flows of itself. As we have often explained, this is the nature of the Oral Torah: the Sages seem to originate its teachings, but they are truly the words of the living God.
וְשִׁבְעָה נֵרוֹתֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ זֶה הַשַּׁבָּת הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ גּוּף הַמְּנוֹרָה שֶׁכּוֹלֵל בְּתוֹכָהּ הַכֹּל כְּמוֹ כֵן שַׁבָּת כּוֹלֵל כָּל שִׁבְעָה הַיָּמִים,
— “‘And its seven lamps upon it’—this is Shabbat”: just as the body of the menorah encompasses everything, Shabbat encompasses all seven days.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב׳ פח א) דְּשַׁבָּת מִתְבָּרְכָאן מִינֵּיהּ כָּל שִׁיתָא יוֹמִין.
— As stated in the holy Zohar (II, 88a), all six days receive blessing from Shabbat.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 30:14: “David said: “Fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.” What does this mean? A person may study Midrash, halakhot, and aggadot, yet if he lacks fear of sin, he possesses nothing. This is like a man who says to his friend, “I have a thousand measures of grain, a thousand of oil, and a thousand of wine.” His friend asks, “Do you have storehouses in which to put them? If so, everything is yours; if not, you have nothing.” So a person studies everything, and they tell him: If you have fear of sin, everything is yours, as it says, “The faithfulness of your times…fear of the Lord is His treasure.” Therefore it says, “Fear of the Lord is pure,” and the prophet cries, “Zion shall be redeemed through justice, and her returnees through righteousness.””

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, 88a (Yitro 27:445–446): “All blessings above and below depend upon the seventh day. Why was no manna found on the seventh day? Because all six supernal days are blessed from that day, and each gives its sustenance below on its own day from the blessing received on the seventh day. Therefore one who abides in faith must arrange his table and prepare a meal on Shabbat night, so that his table may be blessed throughout the six days. At that time blessing is available for all six weekdays, and blessing does not rest upon an empty table. Therefore one must arrange his Shabbat-night table with bread and food.”

p: וּשְׁנַיִם זֵתִים עָלֶיהָ אֶחָד מִימִין הַגּוּלָּה וְאֶחָד עַל שְׂמֹאלָהּ מְרַמֵּז עַל שְׁנֵי אוֹפַנֵּי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בַּתּוֹרָה.
— “And two olive trees beside it, one to the right of the bowl and one to its left” alludes to two forms of effort in Torah.

הָאֶחָד עַל שְׂמֹאלָהּ מְרַמֵּז עַל עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה לַעֲקֹר וּלְשָׁרֵשׁ אֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מֵחָלָל הַשְּׂמָאלִי שֶׁבַּלֵּב וּלְזַכֵּךְ וּלְטַהֵר אֶת הַלֵּב כְּסִיל מֵרְצוֹנִיּוּת וְחֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
— The one on the left alludes to Torah study that uproots the evil inclination from the heart’s left chamber and refines and purifies the foolish heart of worldly desires and cravings.
וְאֶחָד מִימִין מְרַמֵּז שֶׁאַף שֶׁמְּטַהֵר לִבּוֹ מִתַּאֲוֹת וְחֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה צָרִיךְ לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּעֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה לְהַכְנִיס בְּלִבּוֹ קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
— The one on the right alludes to the need, even after purifying the heart of worldly desires and cravings, to labor in Torah study to bring His holiness into one’s heart.

כְּדְאִיתָא (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יח:) אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר לֹא הָלַךְ לְטַרְטִיָּאוֹת וְכוּלֵי וּבְדֶרֶךְ חַטָּאִים לֹא עָמָד זֶה וְכוּלֵי שֶׁמָּא יֹאמַר אָדָם וְכוּלֵי אֵלֵךְ וְאֶתְגָּרֶה בְּשֵׁינָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ יֶהְגֶּה יוֹמָם וָלָיְלָה,

— As taught in Avodah Zarah 18b: “‘Praiseworthy is the man who did not go’—to theaters,” and so forth; “‘and did not stand in the way of sinners’—this,” and so forth. “Lest a person say,” and so forth, “‘I will go and indulge in sleep,’ Scripture says, ‘and he meditates in His Torah day and night.’”

דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁמִּצַּד שֶׁמְּטַהֵר לְבָבוֹ מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע עֲדַיִין לֹא יִקְנֶה קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ רַק עַל יְדֵי עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁמַּכְנִיס קְדוּשָּׁה בַּלֵּב כִּי זֶהוּ תַּכְלִית רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהַכְנִיס בַּלֵּב מַאֲמַר אָנֹכִי שֶׁהוּא יְדִיעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.

— Purifying the heart of the evil inclination does not yet enable one to acquire His holiness. Only Torah study brings holiness into the heart. His ultimate will is to implant within the heart the declaration “I am”—knowledge of Him.
וְרַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי פֵּרֵשׁ עַל פָּסוּק אֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי בְנֵי הַיִּצְהָר קֶרֶן כְּהוּנָּה וּמַלְכוּת הַנִּמְשָׁחִים וְכוּלֵי,
— Rashi explains “these are the two sons of oil” as the eminence of priesthood and kingship, whose holders are anointed, and so forth.
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן מְרַמֵּז עַל שְׁתֵּי בְּחִינוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרוֹת,
— This too alludes to the two aspects just mentioned.

כִּי מַלְכוּת מְרַמֵּז עַל כֹּחַ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה לְנַקּוֹת וּלְטַהֵר הַלֵּב מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע כִּי מֶלֶךְ מְרַמֵּז עַל הַלֵּב וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הַלֵּב מִכָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהוּא הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהוּא לְטַהֵר חָלָל הַשְּׂמָאלִי שֶׁבַּלֵּב מִשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה הַשּׁוֹכֵן שָׁם.

— Kingship alludes to the power of Torah teachings to cleanse and purify the heart of the evil inclination, for the king signifies the heart. King David, peace be upon him, is the heart of all Israel and the man who established the yoke of repentance, purifying the heart’s left chamber of the “leaven in the dough” that dwells there.
וְאִיתָא בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה (פֶּרֶק ו׳) לֵב בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמֶלֶךְ בַּמִּלְחָמָה.
— Sefer Yetzirah, chapter 6, teaches, “The heart in the soul is like a king in battle.”

p: וּכְהוּנָּה מְרַמֵּז עַל עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה לִידִיעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ שֶׁיַּכְנִיס קְדוּשָּׁה בְּלֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ,
— Priesthood alludes to Torah study directed toward knowing Him, blessed be His Name, bringing holiness into “a wise man’s heart at his right.”
וְכַדִּכְתִיב כִּי שִׂפְתֵי כֹהֵן יִשְׁמְרוּ דַעַת וְתוֹרָה יְבַקְשׁוּ מִפִּיהוּ כִּי מַלְאַךְ הַשֵּׁם צְבָאוֹת הוּא וּמַלְאָכִים אֵין לָהֶם יֵצֶר הָרָע.
— As it is written, “For the lips of a priest preserve knowledge, and they seek Torah from his mouth, for he is a messenger of Hashem of Hosts.” Angels have no evil inclination.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁמִּפִּי הַכֹּהֵן הֵם כְּמוֹ מִפִּי מַלְאָךְ שֶׁמְּבוֹרָרִים רַק לִרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּי הַמַּלְאָךְ לֹא יוּכַל לְדַבֵּר רַק דִּבְרֵי הַשֵּׁם.
— The Torah from the priest’s mouth is thus like that from an angel’s mouth, refined to express His will alone, for an angel can speak only Hashem’s words.
וּמַלְכוּת חַשְׁמוֹנָאִים כּוֹלֶלֶת שְׁנֵי מַדְרֵגוֹת עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה כִּי הָיוּ כֹהֲנִים וְגַם מְלָכִים.
— The Hasmonean kingdom encompassed both levels of Torah study, for they were both priests and kings.

p: וְהִנֵּה בַּגְּמָרָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין כד.) וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלַי אֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי בְנֵי הַיִּצְהָר וְגוֹמֵר וּשְׁנַיִם זֵתִים עָלֶיהָ.
— The Gemara (Sanhedrin 24a) discusses “He said to me: These are the two sons of oil,” and so forth, and “two olive trees beside it.”
יִצְהָר אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנּוֹחִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה כְּשֶׁמֶן זַיִת.
— “Oil” refers to the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel, who are as agreeable to one another in halakhic discussion as olive oil.
וּשְׁנַיִם זֵיתִים אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁמְּרִירִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה כַּזַּיִת,
— “Two olive trees” refers to the Torah scholars of Babylonia, who are as bitter toward one another in halakhic discussion as an olive.
וּבַפָּסוּק כְּתִיב וָאוֹמַר אֵלָיו מַה שְּׁנֵי הַזֵּתִים הָאֵלֶּה וְגוֹמֵר וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי בְנֵי הַיִּצְהָר וְגוֹמֵר.
— Yet the verse says, “I said to him: What are these two olive trees?” and so forth, and he replied, “These are the two sons of oil,” and so forth.

וְהִנֵּה הַגְּמָרָא פַּלְגִינְהוּ לְתַרְתֵּי דְּהַזֵּיתִים תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל וּבְנֵי הַיִּצְהָר תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל וַהֲרֵי בַכָּתוּב נֶאֱמַר עַל הַזֵּיתִים אֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי בְנֵי הַיִּצְהָר שֶׁהַמַּשְׁמָעוּת שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֶחָד.

— The Gemara separates them into two groups: the olive trees are the scholars of Babylonia, and the sons of oil are the scholars of the Land of Israel. Yet Scripture identifies the olive trees themselves as the two sons of oil, implying that both are one.
אָכֵן הָעִנְיָן הוּא דְּתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל נוֹחִין זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה שֶׁבִּזְמַן הַבַּיִת לֹא הָיָה מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּין הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים בְּעִנְיַן הֲלָכָה,

— The explanation is that the scholars of the Land of Israel were agreeable to one another in halakhic discussion, because during the Temple period no unresolved halakhic dispute remained among the scholars.
כַּדִּכְתִיב כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר לַמִּשְׁפָּט וְגוֹמֵר וְקַמְתָּ וְעָלִיתָ וְגוֹמֵר וְעָשִׂיתָ עַל פִּי הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יַגִּידוּ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר,
— As it says, “If a matter of judgment is too difficult for you,” and so forth, “you shall rise and ascend,” and so forth, “and you shall act according to the word they tell you,” and so forth.
וּבְעֵת שֶׁהָיָה חִלּוּקֵי דֵעוֹת בֵּין הַחֲכָמִים הָיוּ עוֹלִים לְלִשְׁכַּת הַגָּזִית וְהָיוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין מַכְרִיעִין וְלֹא הָיָה מַחֲלוֹקֶת כְּלָל.
— When the Sages differed, they ascended to the Chamber of Hewn Stone; the Sanhedrin resolved the issue and no dispute remained.
אָמְנָם בְּבָבֶל לֹא נִמְצָא הֲלָכָה בְרוּרָה וְיֵשׁ מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּין הַחֲכָמִים וְאֵין מַכְרִיעַ וּמְרִירִין זֶה לָזֶה כַּזַּיִת,
— In Babylonia, however, the halakhah is not definitively established; the Sages disagree, with no final arbiter, and are bitter toward one another like an olive.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא לְעֵיל מִינָּהּ חוֹבְלִים אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁמְּחַבְּלִים זֶה לָזֶה בַּהֲלָכָה כִּי בִּשְׁעַת הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת הֵם כְּשׂוֹנְאִים זֶה לָזֶה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (קִידּוּשִׁין ל:) אֲפִלּוּ הָאָב וּבְנוֹ וְכוּלֵי,

— As the Gemara states just before this, “Destroyers” means the scholars of Babylonia, who assail one another in halakhic discussion. During the dispute they seem like enemies, as taught in Kiddushin 30b, “Even a father and his son,” and so forth.
אֲבָל גַּם בָּהֶם כְּתִיב אֶת וָהֵב בְּסוּפָה אַהֲבָה בְּסוֹפָהּ מֵחֲמַת כִּי הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת הִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
— Yet of them too it says “Et Vahev beSufah”—love at its conclusion—because their dispute is for the sake of Heaven.

paragraphs.text: Deuteronomy 17:8-11: “If a matter of judgment is too difficult for you—between blood and blood, between claim and claim, between affliction and affliction, matters of dispute within your gates—you shall arise and go up to the place that Hashem your God will choose. You shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who will be in those days; inquire, and they will tell you the matter of judgment. You shall act according to the word they tell you from that place which Hashem will choose, taking care to do all that they instruct you. According to the Torah they teach you and the judgment they tell you, you shall act. Do not turn aside from the word they tell you, to the right or to the left.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 25:6: “In truth, in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which instruction went forth, there was no dispute; only afterward, in Babylonia, did the essential dispute begin, the ‘wars of Hashem’ in the Oral Torah. So it is expounded: ‘Oil’—the Torah scholars of the Land of Israel, who are agreeable to one another in halakhah like olive oil; ‘two olive trees beside it’—the Torah scholars of Babylonia, who are bitter toward one another in halakhah like an olive. — The question, “What are these two olive trees?” and so forth,

הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (חֲגִיגָה ג:) בַּעֲלֵי אֲסוּפּוֹת אֵלּוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין אֲסוּפּוֹת אֲסוּפּוֹת וְעוֹסְקִין בַּתּוֹרָה הַלָּלוּ מְטַמְּאִין וְהַלָּלוּ מְטַהֲרִין וְכוּלֵי שֶׁמָּא יֹאמַר אָדָם הֵיאַךְ אֲנִי לָמֵד תּוֹרָה מֵעַתָּה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר כּוּלָּם נִתְּנוּ מֵרוֹעֶה אֶחָד אֵל אֶחָד נְתָנָן פַּרְנָס אֶחָד אֲמָרָן וְכוּלֵי,

— parallels the teaching in Chagigah 3b: “‘Masters of assemblies’—these are Torah scholars who sit in groups studying Torah; some declare impure and others pure,” and so forth. “Lest a person ask, ‘How, then, can I study Torah?’ Scripture says, ‘All were given by one Shepherd’: one God gave them, one leader spoke them,” and so forth.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר מַה שְּׁנֵי הַזֵּיתִים שֶׁמְּרִירִין זֶה לָזֶה מִצַּד הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בֵּינֵיהֶם וְלֹא נִמְצָא הֲלָכָה בְרוּרָה וְהֵיאַךְ אֲנִי לָמֵד תּוֹרָה מֵעַתָּה,
— Thus he asked: What are these two olive trees, bitter toward each other because of their disputes, leaving no definitive halakhah—how can I now study Torah?

וְעַל זֶה הֱשִׁיבוֹ הַמַּלְאָךְ אַל תִּתְמַהּ עַל זֶה כִּי אֵלֶּה הֵם בְּנֵי הַיִּצְהָר הַיְינוּ שֶׁגַּם הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּבָבֶל שֶׁיֵּשׁ מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּינֵיהֶם נֶחְשָׁבִים גַּם כֵּן בְּנֵי הַיִּצְהָר כְּתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת מִפִּי אֲדוֹן כָּל הַמַּעֲשִׂים בָּרוּךְ הוּא.

— The angel answered: Do not wonder at this, for these are the sons of oil. The scholars of Babylonia, despite their disagreements, are also regarded as sons of oil like the scholars of the Land of Israel, for both views are the words of the living God, and both are true, from the mouth of the Master of all deeds, blessed be He.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkat HaTzadik §186: “This is why fear is necessary; as is known, judgments are aroused from binah. Every new interpretation carries the fear that, Heaven forbid, it may be false. Hence the introduction to the Zohar says not to innovate something one has not heard from one’s teacher. Accordingly, the Sages stipulated that those who sharpen one another must act for the sake of Heaven and with humility. Then they succeed, for even in their disagreement, ‘these and those are the words of the living God.’ It is a union, like the dispute of Shammai and Hillel, whose end is to endure, rather than a falsehood that ceases, like strife that separates brothers. Therefore, ‘binah is the heart,’ where fear resides. … Shabbat, however, is rest: when they act for the sake of Heaven, ‘love is at the end’; they unite together and join in zimmun.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The qualification “for the sake of Heaven and with humility” explains how conflicting Torah positions can remain a union. Rav Tzadok’s parallel also links their eventual reconciliation to Shabbat’s rest, clarifying the manuscript’s comparison of the disputing Babylonian scholars to the “sons of oil.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Ritva on Eruvin 13b, s.v. “Both these and those”: ““Both these and those are the words of the living God.” The rabbis of France, of blessed memory, asked: How is it possible that both are the words of the living God, when one forbids and the other permits? They answered that when Moses ascended on high to receive the Torah, he was shown forty-nine aspects of prohibition and forty-nine aspects of permission for each matter. He asked the Holy One, blessed be He, about this, and He said that it would be entrusted to the sages of Israel in every generation, and the decision would follow them. This is correct according to the homiletical approach; according to the way of truth, there is a mystical explanation for the matter.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The Ritva explains how the opposed positions can both come from “the Master of all deeds”: revelation itself contains the different aspects that the sages develop. Their divine origin does not eliminate the need for a ruling; the decision is entrusted to the sages of each generation. This clarifies the distinction between Rav Tzadok’s affirmation that both positions are true and the question of which position determines practice.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 5:7: “This is the teaching of the miracle of the oil. At the close of the years of Yose ben Yoezer, who was killed in the Greek decrees, the Sages sensed that ‘the heart had diminished,’ as stated in the Gemara: only the lowest level remained in the souls of Israel, the lower awe that comes from faith. The single cruse of oil, with enough to burn for only one day, alludes to this single attribute, the Kingdom of Heaven. A miracle was done with it and they lit from it for eight days: the light grew until it reached the eighth level, awe absorbed in the innermost point of the heart. … This is the meaning of what Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said on ‘The words of the wise … masters of assemblies’: ‘These declare impure and these declare pure … all were given by one Shepherd; one God gave them.’ That is, even now that hearts have diminished, the heart can still acquire the power to unite even differing opinions, so that they become ‘everything that He made, and behold, it was very good.’”
